title: 学术综合任务与转段检查 · Four listening sections
instructions: 原创模拟训练材料；先独立作答，再核对依据。四节音频共40题，按顺序听音作答。合成训练音频时长不同于正式考试。
transcript:
Section 1: Library Study Room Booking

M: Good morning, City Library. How can I help you?
W: Hello. I'd like to book a study room for next week, please. I'm planning to work on a project with a friend, and we'd prefer a quiet space rather than the open reading area, because the open area can get quite noisy in the afternoons, especially when lots of people are studying there at the same time. A private room would help us concentrate better.
M: Certainly. We have several study rooms on the second floor, and they are popular with students, so it's a good idea to book ahead. Which day would you like?
W: Wednesday, the 15th. In the afternoon if possible.
M: Let me check the booking system. We have a room available from 2 to 4 p.m. Is that suitable?
W: Yes, that's fine. How much does it cost?
M: It's free for students, but there's a small charge for non-students. Are you a student?
W: Yes, I'm a postgraduate student at the university.
M: Great. Then it's free. Can I have your name and student number?
W: My name is Li Wei, and my student number is 20231567.
M: Thank you. And how many people will be in the room?
W: Just two of us. My friend and I are working on a project together.
M: Okay. We usually allow up to four people per room, so that's fine. Do you need any equipment?
W: Yes, we need a whiteboard and a projector.
M: I can book those for you. The projector is an extra 5 pounds, but the whiteboard is free.
W: That's okay. We'll take both.
M: Alright. So that's Wednesday the 15th, 2 to 4 p.m., room 204, with a whiteboard and projector. Is there anything else?
W: Actually, can we extend the booking to 5 p.m.? We might need more time to finish our work.
M: Let me see... Yes, the room is free until 5. So I'll change it to 2 to 5 p.m. That will be an extra 2 pounds for the projector, making it 7 pounds in total.
W: That's fine. Thank you.
M: You're welcome. Please arrive on time, as the room is booked by another group at 5:30.
W: We will. Thanks for your help.
M: You're welcome. Have a good day.

Section 2: Academic Task Week 36: Listening Part 2 – Campus Orientation for Visiting Students

Hello everyone, and welcome to Northbridge University. My name is Sarah, and I’m the student services coordinator. I’ll give you some practical information about your first week here. Please listen carefully, because some details are important for your registration, and missing them could cause unnecessary problems later.

First, orientation begins on Monday at 9 a.m. in the Main Hall. You need to bring your passport and your acceptance letter. If you don’t have your acceptance letter, go to the admissions office before 8:30 a.m. They will print a copy for you, so please allow enough time and arrive early to avoid queues. The orientation will finish at 12:30 p.m., and lunch will be provided in the dining hall. During orientation you will also meet your academic advisers and receive key information about module choices, so it is essential that you attend the whole session.

Now, about your student ID cards. You can collect them from the library on Tuesday between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. You must bring a passport-sized photo. The card is free, but if you lose it, a replacement costs fifteen pounds. Please keep it safe, because you will need it throughout your studies—for example, to borrow books, enter buildings, and use the sports centre.

Next, the campus tour. There are two tours: one at 2 p.m. on Monday and another at 10 a.m. on Wednesday. Each tour lasts about one hour. The tour starts from the main entrance, not from the library. I repeat: the meeting point is the main entrance. The tour covers the library, the sports centre, and the student union building. It does not go to the medical centre, so if you need to find the doctor, ask at the reception desk.

Regarding your timetable, you will receive it by email on Wednesday evening. Check your university email account, not your personal one. If you have any problems with your timetable, contact your department secretary. Do not email me directly, because I cannot change your timetable.

Finally, the welcome party is on Friday at 6 p.m. in the student union building. It is free for all new students. You can bring one guest, but you must register your guest by Thursday noon. There will be food and music. I hope you enjoy your time here. Thank you.

Section 3: Academic Group Project: Mid-Project Review

TUTOR: Good morning, both. Thanks for coming in for this mid-project review. Let's start with a quick update. How's the group project going?

STUDENT A (Maya): Well, we've finished the literature review, and we're now collecting data from the surveys. But we've had a few problems with the questionnaire design.

TUTOR: OK. What kind of problems?

STUDENT A: Some questions were ambiguous. For example, we asked 'How often do you study?' but we didn't give clear options like 'daily' or 'weekly'. So the answers were inconsistent.

STUDENT B (Leo): That's true. Also, we realised that we hadn't piloted the questionnaire before sending it out. That was a mistake.

TUTOR: Right. Piloting is essential because it helps you identify unclear questions and technical issues before the main data collection. So what have you done about it?

STUDENT B: We've revised the questions and we're going to test them with a small group of ten students tomorrow.

TUTOR: Good. Now, about the data analysis. Have you decided on the statistical tests?

STUDENT A: Not yet. We were thinking of using a t-test, but we're not sure if the data is normally distributed.

TUTOR: You should check that first. If it's not normal, you might need a non-parametric test. Also, remember to report effect sizes, not just p-values, as they show the practical significance of your findings.

STUDENT B: OK, we'll do that. Another thing: we're struggling with the timeline. We have only three weeks left, and we still need to write the discussion section.

TUTOR: Let's prioritise. The discussion is crucial. I suggest you draft it while you're waiting for the pilot results. And don't forget to reference properly – I noticed some missing citations in your last draft.

STUDENT A: Yes, we'll fix that. We're also planning to meet twice a week from now on.

TUTOR: That sounds sensible. One more thing: have you considered the ethical approval? You need it before you can use the data from the pilot.

STUDENT B: Oh, we didn't know that. We'll apply for it today.

TUTOR: Good. So, to summarise: revise the questionnaire, pilot it, check data distribution, draft the discussion, and get ethical approval. Is that everything?

STUDENT A: I think so. Thank you.

TUTOR: You're welcome. Keep me updated.

Section 4: Academic Listening: The Role of Sleep in Memory Consolidation

Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about something that affects all of us: sleep, and specifically its role in memory consolidation. Now, you might think that sleep is just a time for the body to rest, but research over the past two decades has shown that sleep is actively involved in processing and storing information. In this lecture, I'll explain how sleep helps consolidate memory, discuss the different stages of sleep involved, and finally consider some practical implications for students.

First, let's define memory consolidation. It's the process by which newly acquired information is stabilized and integrated into long-term memory. Without consolidation, memories would remain fragile and easily forgotten. So, how does sleep contribute? During sleep, the brain replays patterns of neural activity that occurred during learning. This replay strengthens the connections between neurons, a phenomenon known as synaptic plasticity. In other words, sleep helps to 'lock in' what we've learned.

Now, not all sleep stages are equally important. Deep sleep, or slow-wave sleep, which occurs mostly in the first half of the night, is crucial for consolidating factual information, like dates or vocabulary. REM sleep, on the other hand, which is more prevalent in the second half of the night, seems to be important for procedural memory, such as learning a new skill or a sport. So, if you're studying for an exam that requires memorizing facts, you might want to ensure you get enough deep sleep early in the night. But if you're learning to play the piano, REM sleep later in the night might be more beneficial.

Let me give you an example. A study by Smith and colleagues in 2019 found that participants who slept for eight hours after learning a list of words remembered 20% more words than those who stayed awake for the same period. Interestingly, the researchers also found that the sleep group showed greater activation in the hippocampus during a recall test. This suggests that sleep not only preserves memories but also enhances their accessibility.

However, it's not just the amount of sleep that matters; the quality is also important. Frequent interruptions during sleep can reduce the benefits. For instance, people with sleep apnea, a condition where breathing stops briefly during sleep, often report memory problems. So, if you're a student, try to maintain a regular sleep schedule and create a dark, quiet environment.

In conclusion, sleep is not a passive state but an active process that helps consolidate both factual and procedural memories. By understanding how sleep works, we can optimize our learning strategies. Thank you for listening, and I'm happy to take any questions now.

grammar.title: 时态、从句、冠词、数量和主谓一致复习
grammar.explanation: 本部分复习五个语法点：1) 时态：对话中使用了多种时态，如一般现在时（I'm planning）、一般将来时（I'll change it）、现在进行时（are studying）等。2) 从句：如“because the open area can get quite noisy”是原因状语从句。3) 冠词：定冠词the和不定冠词a/an的使用。4) 数量：如“two of us”、“four people”。5) 主谓一致：主语和谓语动词在人称和数上保持一致。
grammar.example: W: Just two of us. My friend and I are working on a project together.

questions.evidence: The number of students is increasing.
